claim: Voltage-gated Na+ channels (VGSCs) in peripheral sensory neurons are essential for the pain and hypersensitivity associated with tissue injury.
source: Available evidence indicates voltage-gated Na+ channels (VGSCs) in peripheral sensory neurons are essential for the pain and hypersensitivity associated with tissue injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to existing literature, as indicated by the phrase 'Available evidence indicates'.

claim: Expression systems influence the biophysical and pharmacological properties of VGSCs.
source: However, our understanding of the biophysical and pharmacological properties of the channels in sensory neurons is largely based on the study of heterologous systems or rodent tissue, despite evidence that both expression systems and species differences influence these properties.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that evidence exists showing expression systems influence channel properties.

claim: Species differences influence the biophysical and pharmacological properties of VGSCs.
source: However, our understanding of the biophysical and pharmacological properties of the channels in sensory neurons is largely based on the study of heterologous systems or rodent tissue, despite evidence that both expression systems and species differences influence these properties.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that evidence exists showing species differences influence channel properties.

claim: Two major current types exist in human DRG neurons: tetrodotoxin (TTX)-sensitive and TTX-resistant currents.
source: Our results indicate that while the two major current types, generally referred to as tetrodotoxin (TTX)-sensitive and TTX-resistant were qualitatively similar in neurons from rats and humans, there were several differences that have important implications for drug development as well as our understanding of pain mechanisms.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: TTX-sensitive and TTX-resistant currents are qualitatively similar in neurons from rats and humans.
source: Our results indicate that while the two major current types, generally referred to as tetrodotoxin (TTX)-sensitive and TTX-resistant were qualitatively similar in neurons from rats and humans, there were several differences that have important implications for drug development as well as our understanding of pain mechanisms.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: There are several differences between rat and human DRG neuron Na+ currents that have important implications for drug development and understanding of pain mechanisms.
source: Our results indicate that while the two major current types, generally referred to as tetrodotoxin (TTX)-sensitive and TTX-resistant were qualitatively similar in neurons from rats and humans, there were several differences that have important implications for drug development as well as our understanding of pain mechanisms.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Voltage-gated Na+ channels underlie the upstroke of the action potential.
source: It has long been appreciated that voltage-gated Na+ channels (VGSCs) underlie the upstroke of the action potential, and therefore play an essential role in the propagation of action potentials along axons (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952a, 1952b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hodgkin and Huxley's foundational work.

claim: VGSCs play an essential role in the propagation of action potentials along axons.
source: It has long been appreciated that voltage-gated Na+ channels (VGSCs) underlie the upstroke of the action potential, and therefore play an essential role in the propagation of action potentials along axons (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952a, 1952b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hodgkin and Huxley's foundational work.

claim: VGSCs consist of an alpha subunit responsible for all essential features of a functional channel and up to two beta subunits that influence channel density and/or gating properties.
source: VGSCs consist of an alpha subunit, responsible for all essential features of a functional channel and up to two beta subunits that influence channel density and/or gating properties (Yu et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2005.

claim: Nine alpha subunits and four beta subunits of VGSCs have been identified.
source: Nine alpha subunits and four beta subunits have been identified.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Changes in the biophysical properties of VGSCs contribute to the dynamic regulation of neuronal excitability.
source: VGSCs have remained a target for the development of novel therapeutics because it is now also appreciated that changes in the biophysical properties (Cantrell and Catterall, 2001), distribution (Cusdin et al., 2008; Kuba et al., 2010), and/or expression (Aptowicz et al., 2004; Qiao et al., 2013) of these channels contributes to the dynamic regulation of neuronal excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Changes in the distribution of VGSCs contribute to the dynamic regulation of neuronal excitability.
source: VGSCs have remained a target for the development of novel therapeutics because it is now also appreciated that changes in the biophysical properties (Cantrell and Catterall, 2001), distribution (Cusdin et al., 2008; Kuba et al., 2010), and/or expression (Aptowicz et al., 2004; Qiao et al., 2013) of these channels contributes to the dynamic regulation of neuronal excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Changes in the expression of VGSCs contribute to the dynamic regulation of neuronal excitability.
source: VGSCs have remained a target for the development of novel therapeutics because it is now also appreciated that changes in the biophysical properties (Cantrell and Catterall, 2001), distribution (Cusdin et al., 2008; Kuba et al., 2010), and/or expression (Aptowicz et al., 2004; Qiao et al., 2013) of these channels contributes to the dynamic regulation of neuronal excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Phosphorylation-dependent increases in Na+ current underlie acute increases in nociceptor excitability associated with inflammation.
source: Such changes have been particularly well documented in the context of pain, where both phosphorylation-dependent increases in Na+ current, as well as more persistent increases in VGSC expression, have been shown to underlie both the acute and persistent increases in nociceptor excitability associated with inflammation (Gold et al., 1996; Gould et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gold et al., 1996 and Gould et al., 1998.

claim: Persistent increases in VGSC expression underlie persistent increases in nociceptor excitability associated with inflammation.
source: Such changes have been particularly well documented in the context of pain, where both phosphorylation-dependent increases in Na+ current, as well as more persistent increases in VGSC expression, have been shown to underlie both the acute and persistent increases in nociceptor excitability associated with inflammation (Gold et al., 1996; Gould et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gold et al., 1996 and Gould et al., 1998.

claim: Ongoing pain and hypersensitivity associated with peripheral nerve injury are associated with changes in the pattern of VGSC expression.
source: Similarly, both the ongoing pain and hypersensitivity associated with peripheral nerve injury are associated with changes in the pattern of VGSC expression (Gold et al., 2003; Waxman et al., 1994; Hunter et al., 1997) as well as distribution of channels in peripheral nerves (Gold et al., 2003; Henry et al., 2007; Tseng et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Ongoing pain and hypersensitivity associated with peripheral nerve injury are associated with changes in the distribution of channels in peripheral nerves.
source: Similarly, both the ongoing pain and hypersensitivity associated with peripheral nerve injury are associated with changes in the pattern of VGSC expression (Gold et al., 2003; Waxman et al., 1994; Hunter et al., 1997) as well as distribution of channels in peripheral nerves (Gold et al., 2003; Henry et al., 2007; Tseng et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Several VGSC alpha subunits that contribute to injury-induced increases in afferent excitability are preferentially expressed in the peripheral nervous system and nociceptive afferents.
source: From a therapeutic perspective, what has been particularly exciting about the evidence implicating VGSCs in inflammatory and neuropathic pain, is that several of the VGSC alpha subunits shown to contribute to the injury-induced increases in afferent excitability are preferentially expressed in the peripheral nervous system in general, and nociceptive afferents in particular (Gold and Gebhart, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gold and Gebhart, 2010.

claim: A VGSC subtype specific blocker could provide effective pain relief with minimal side effects.
source: This has raised the intriguing possibility that a VGSC subtype specific blocker would provide effective pain relief with minimal side effects.
evidence: This is presented as a logical inference from the preferential expression of certain VGSC subtypes in nociceptive afferents.

claim: Evidence of a role of VGSCs in pain states obtained with pre-clinical rodent models has been confirmed in pain patients.
source: Evidence in support of a role of VGSCs in a variety of pain states obtained with pre-clinical, largely rodent models, has been confirmed in pain patients.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, though no specific citations are provided in this sentence.

claim: Genetic and anatomical evidence suggests that VGSC alpha and beta subunits and their pattern of expression are similar in rodents and humans.
source: Similarly, genetic and anatomical evidence suggests that the VGSC alpha and beta subunits, and their pattern of expression, are similar in rodents and man.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, though no specific citations are provided in this sentence.

claim: Virtually all knowledge about the biophysical and pharmacological properties of VGSCs comes from the study of heterologous expression systems and isolated rodent sensory neurons.
source: Nevertheless, virtually all that is known about the biophysical and pharmacological properties of VGSCs comes from the study of these channels in heterologous expression systems and in isolated rodent sensory neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Co-expression of VGSC beta1 and beta2-subunits with the alpha subunit NaV1.2 in frog oocytes increases current density and the rate of current inactivation.
source: For example, co-expression of VGSC beta1 and beta2-subunits with the alpha subunit NaV1.2 in frog oocytes not only increases current density, but the rate of current inactivation (Patton et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Patton et al., 1994.

claim: VGSC beta1 and beta2-subunits have no influence on current density or inactivation when co-expressed with NaV1.2 in tsA-201 cells.
source: In contrast, these beta-subunits have no influence on either current density or inactivation when co-expressed with NaV1.2 in tsA-201 cells (Qu et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Qu et al., 2001.

claim: In tsA-201 cells, VGSC beta-subunits drive a rightward shift in the voltage-dependence of NaV1.2 channel activation.
source: Rather, in tsA-201 cells, the beta-subunits drive a rightward shift in the voltage-dependence of channel activation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the literature, following the citation to Qu et al., 2001.

claim: A-803467 is over three orders of magnitude more potent against heterologously expressed human NaV1.8 than four of the other nine human alpha subunits tested.
source: Similarly, the putatively NaV1.8 selective blocker A-803467 is over three orders of magnitude more potent against heterologously expressed human NaV1.8 than four of the other nine human alpha subunits tested, yet is only half as potent against the current believed to reflect activation of NaV1.8 channels, natively expressed in rat dorsal root ganglion neurons (Jarvis et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jarvis et al., 2007.

claim: A-803467 is only half as potent against the current believed to reflect activation of NaV1.8 channels natively expressed in rat dorsal root ganglion neurons compared to heterologously expressed human NaV1.8.
source: Similarly, the putatively NaV1.8 selective blocker A-803467 is over three orders of magnitude more potent against heterologously expressed human NaV1.8 than four of the other nine human alpha subunits tested, yet is only half as potent against the current believed to reflect activation of NaV1.8 channels, natively expressed in rat dorsal root ganglion neurons (Jarvis et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jarvis et al., 2007.

claim: Neurons included in this study were obtained from 21 donors (13 males and 8 females).
source: Neurons included in this study were obtained from 21 donors (13 males and 8 females).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study's methodology and sample.

claim: The average age of the donors was 45.2 years with a range of 13 to 77.
source: The average age of the donors was 45.2 years with a range of 13 to 77.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study's methodology and sample.

claim: At least one data point was obtained from a total of 226 neurons that met inclusion criteria for clamp control and holding current.
source: At least one data point was obtained from a total of 226 neurons that met inclusion criteria for clamp control and holding current.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study's methodology and sample.

claim: It is possible to use voltage-clamp protocols to isolate the rapidly activating rapidly inactivating putative TTX sensitive (TTX-S) Na+ current from the more slowly activating and slowly inactivating TTX-resistant (TTX-R) Na+ current.
source: In order to maximize the amount of data collected from each neuron, we first determined whether it was possible to use voltage-clamp protocols to isolate the rapidly activating rapidly inactivating putative TTX sensitive (TTX-S) Na+ current from the more slowly activating and slowly inactivating TTX-resistant (TTX-R) Na+ current, as we have previously done in the rat (Gold et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, with reference to previous work in rats.

claim: Currents isolated with voltage-clamp protocols were identical to those isolated with TTX.
source: We subsequently confirmed that currents isolated in this manner were identical to those isolated with TTX (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The fast component of the current was inactivated over a range of test potentials more hyperpolarized than the range of test potential over which the slow component of the current was inactivated.
source: The fast component of the current evoked at 0 mV (open circles), was inactivated over a range of test potentials more hyperpolarized than the range of test potential over which the slow component of the current evoked at 0 mV (closed circles) was inactivated.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Application of 300 nM TTX removed the same component of the total current as the test pulse to −40 mV.
source: Application of 300 nM TTX removed the same component of the total current as the test pulse to −40 mV.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The difference between the total current and the current evoked at −40 mV, or that evoked in the presence of 300 mM TTX is virtually identical.
source: The difference between the total current and the current evoked at −40 mV, or that evoked in the presence of 300 mM TTX is virtually identical.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Small to medium diameter DRG neurons from both human and rat were initially focused on because neurons with a small to medium cell body diameter are more likely to give rise to slowly conducting axons, which are more likely to be nociceptive.
source: We initially focused on the small to medium diameter DRG neurons from both human and rat in this study for two main reasons. First, because the study of Na+ channels in sensory neurons has largely been in the context of pain. In this context, data from guinea pig and rodents suggest that neurons with a small to medium cell body diameter are more likely to give rise to slowly conducting axons (Lawson, 2002), which are, in turn, more likely to be nociceptive.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the study design, supported by a citation to Lawson, 2002.

claim: It was more difficult to maintain clamp control over the currents evoked from human sensory neurons with a larger cell body diameter.
source: Second, it was more difficult to maintain clamp control over the currents evoked from human sensory neurons with a larger cell body diameter.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the study design, based on experimental observations.

claim: Human DRG neuron cell body sizes were relatively normally distributed, in contrast to the skewed, clearly bimodal distribution of DRG neuron cell body sizes previously described in rodents.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to the skewed, clearly bimodal distribution of DRG neuron cell body sizes previously described in rodents (i.e., see [Lawson et al., 1993]), human DRG neuron cell body sizes were relatively normally distributed.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 2A inset, and contrasted with previous rodent data.

claim: The average membrane capacitance of all the neurons included in this study was 116 pF (or ~60 ± 0.8 μm in diameter), with a range from 23 to 255 pF (or 26 to 90 μm).
source: The average membrane capacitance of all the neurons included in this study was 116 pF (or ~60 ± 0.8 μm in diameter), with a range from 23 to 255 pF (or 26 to 90 μm).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental measurements.

claim: Human DRG neurons are significantly larger than small to medium (cell body diameter < 35 μm) rat DRG neurons.
source: As expected, human DRG neurons are significantly larger than small to medium (cell body diameter < 35 μm) rat DRG neurons, which had an average cell body capacitance of 36 pF, with a range of 22 to 70 pF (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No TTX-R current was detected in rat neurons with a cell body capacitance >55 pF.
source: Consistent with previous evidence from the rat suggesting that TTX-R currents are enriched in nociceptive afferents (Djouhri et al., 2003), which tend to have a small cell body diameter (Lawson, 2002), no TTX-R current was detected in rat neurons with a cell body capacitance >55 pF.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, consistent with previous literature.

claim: There was no correlation between human DRG neuron cell body diameter and TTX-R current density.
source: Conversely, there was no correlation (p>0.05) between human DRG neuron cell body diameter and TTX-R current density, or the ratio of TTX-S to TTX-R current, and TTX-R currents were present in the largest neuron studied.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on statistical analysis.

claim: There was no correlation between human DRG neuron cell body diameter and the ratio of TTX-S to TTX-R current.
source: Conversely, there was no correlation (p>0.05) between human DRG neuron cell body diameter and TTX-R current density, or the ratio of TTX-S to TTX-R current, and TTX-R currents were present in the largest neuron studied.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on statistical analysis.

claim: TTX-R currents were present in the largest human neuron studied.
source: Conversely, there was no correlation (p>0.05) between human DRG neuron cell body diameter and TTX-R current density, or the ratio of TTX-S to TTX-R current, and TTX-R currents were present in the largest neuron studied.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: The average capacitance of the nine neurons studied in which only TTX-S current was detected was 83.2 ± 18 pF, which was smaller (p=0.059) than that of the population of neurons with both TTX-S and TTX-R currents.
source: Furthermore, the average capacitance of the nine neurons studied in which only TTX-S current was detected, 83.2 ± 18 pF, was, if anything, smaller (p=0.059), than that of the population of neurons with both TTX-S and TTX-R currents.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on statistical analysis.

claim: The density of both TTX-R and TTX-S current were significantly larger in neurons from human compared to those in rat neurons.
source: Despite normalizing for the differences in cell body capacitance, the density of both TTX-R and TTX-S current were significantly larger in neurons from human (−53.2 ± 6.8 pA/pF (n = 114) and −62.2 ± 4.3 pA/pF (n = 78), respectively) compared to those in rat neurons (−47.7 ± 3.3 pA/pF (n = 26) and −42.6 ± 4.6 pA/pF (n = 26), respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on statistical comparison.

claim: The ratio of TTX-S to TTX-R current density was significantly greater in human than rat DRG neurons.
source: Furthermore, the ratio of TTX-S to TTX-R current density was significantly greater in human than rat DRG neurons (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: TTX-R currents in human DRG neurons were increased within seconds following bath application of inflammatory soup in 13 of 17 neurons tested, resulting in an average increase in peak current of 15 ± 1%.
source: Consistent with previous results from rat and subsequently mouse sensory neurons (Yang and Gereau, 2004), TTX-R currents were increased within seconds following bath application of inflammatory soup (Figure 3). This increase saturated within ~90 s. Comparable results were obtained in 13 of 17 human neurons tested, resulting in an average increase in peak current of 15 ± 1%.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Inflammatory soup application increased rates of TTX-R current activation and inactivation by 9 ± 0.8% and 12 ± 3%, respectively, in human DRG neurons.
source: Concomitantly, rates of current activation and inactivation were increased, 9 ± 0.8% and 12 ± 3%, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: Both the increase in peak TTX-R current and the increase in current activation rate would contribute to an increase in excitability.
source: Both the increase in peak current and the increase in current activation rate would contribute to an increase in excitability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes in current properties.

claim: The increase in TTX-S current following inflammatory soup application was not associated with changes in rates of current activation or inactivation.
source: However, in contrast to TTX-R currents, the increase in TTX-S current was not associated with changes in rates of current activation or inactivation.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: The steady-state properties of TTX-R currents in rat DRG neurons were qualitatively similar to those in human DRG neurons.
source: The steady-state properties of TTX-R currents in rat DRG neurons were qualitatively similar to those in human DRG neurons.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on comparison of data.

claim: Persistent TTX-R currents at −10 and 0 mV were significantly larger in rat neurons than in human neurons.
source: However, in contrast to previous results indicating that persistent TTX-R currents were larger in human DRG neurons (Han et al., 2015), we observed the opposite (Figure 4A and B), where the persistent current in rat neurons at −10 and 0 mV was significantly larger than that in human neurons (Figure 4C, p<0.01 two-way ANOVA with Holm-Sidak post hoc test).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 4, and contrasted with previous literature.

claim: The V0.5 of both inactivation and activation of TTX-R currents were more hyperpolarized in human neurons compared to rat neurons.
source: There were also small but significant differences in the V0.5 of both inactivation (Figure 4D), and activation (Figure 4E), which were more hyperpolarized in human neurons (p<0.01).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: Recovery from inactivation of TTX-R currents was comparably rapid in neurons from both human and rat.
source: In contrast, recovery from inactivation (Figure 4F) was comparably rapid in neurons from both human and rat.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The kinetic properties of TTX-R currents in neurons from rat and human were qualitatively similar with comparable rates of current activation and inactivation.
source: The kinetic properties of TTX-R currents in neurons from rat and human were also qualitatively similar (Figure 5A and B) with comparable rates of current activation (Figure 5C) and inactivation (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: 1 μM A-803467 produced small but consistent block of TTX-R current in human DRG neurons.
source: It was only at the very highest concentration tested (1 μM), that small but consistent block of TTX-R current was observed (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 1 μM A-803467 blocked over 50% of TTX-R current in rat DRG neurons.
source: The same concentration of A-803467 blocked over 50% of TTX-R current in rat DRG neurons (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The difference in fractional block of TTX-R current by 1 μM A-803467 between human and rat was statistically significant.
source: The difference in fractional block between human and rat obtained with this concentration was statistically significant (Figure 6C, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The potency of lidocaine against resting TTX-R currents was comparable in rat and human DRG neurons.
source: The potency of lidocaine was comparable against resting TTX-R currents from rat and human DRG neurons (Figure 7A,B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: TTX-R currents from human DRG neurons demonstrated little use-dependent inactivation in the absence of lidocaine.
source: However, not only did TTX-R currents from human DRG neurons demonstrate little use-dependent inactivation in the absence of lidocaine, there was no detectable use-dependent block of these currents in the presence of lidocaine (Figure 7A and D).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: There was no detectable use-dependent block of TTX-R currents from human DRG neurons in the presence of lidocaine.
source: However, not only did TTX-R currents from human DRG neurons demonstrate little use-dependent inactivation in the absence of lidocaine, there was no detectable use-dependent block of these currents in the presence of lidocaine (Figure 7A and D).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: TTX-R currents in rat DRG neurons showed use-dependent inactivation and block in the absence and presence of lidocaine, respectively.
source: This was in contrast to the use-dependent inactivation and block of TTX-R currents in rat DRG neurons in the absence and presence of lidocaine, respectively (Figure 7B and D, p<0.01 two-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: TTX-S currents in rat and human DRG neurons were qualitatively similar.
source: As with TTX-R currents, TTX-S currents in rat and human DRG neurons were qualitatively similar.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on comparison of data.

claim: There was no significant difference between species with respect to the steady-state inactivation of TTX-S currents.
source: There was also no significant difference between species with respect to the steady-state inactivation of TTX-S currents (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The voltage-dependence of TTX-S activation was significantly more hyperpolarized in human than in rat DRG neurons.
source: However, the voltage-dependence of TTX-S activation was significantly more hyperpolarized in human than in rat DRG neurons (Figure 8B, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Over 80% of TTX-S current from human DRG neurons recovered from inactivation with a fast time-constant, while only 50% of TTX-S current from rat DRG neurons recovered as rapidly.
source: Furthermore, while over 80% of TTX-S current from human DRG neurons recovered from inactivation with a fast time-constant, only 50% of TTX-S current from rat DRG neurons recovered as rapidly (Figure 8C, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: TTX-S current kinetics in neurons from rat and human were qualitatively similar.
source: TTX-S current kinetics in neurons from rat and human were also qualitatively similar (Figure 9A - D).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 9.

claim: TTX-S current activation rate in human DRG neurons was faster than that in rat DRG neurons across the voltage range of current activation that was tested.
source: However, current activation rate in human DRG neurons was faster than that in rat DRG neurons across the voltage range of current activation that was tested (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Only ~30% of the TTX-S current in human DRG neurons was blocked by 30 nM TTX, in contrast to the >90% of current blocked in rat DRG neurons.
source: Consistent with this impression, there was a significant difference between TTX-S currents from rat and human DRG neurons with respect to the fraction of current blocked by 30 nM TTX. That is, only ~30% of the TTX-S current in human DRG neurons was blocked by this concentration of TTX (Figure 10A) in contrast to the >90% of current blocked in rat DRG neurons (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The fractional block of TTX-S current produced by 30 nM TTX was significantly greater in rat than in human DRG neurons.
source: This difference was statistically significant (Figure 10C, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Lidocaine was less potent against resting TTX-S current in rat than in human DRG neurons.
source: In contrast to the results obtained with TTX-R currents, there were differences between rat and human DRG neurons with respect to the resting block of TTX-S current, where lidocaine was less potent in the rat than the human (Figure 11A,B and C, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 11.

claim: TTX-S currents in neurons from both rat and human were subject to use-dependent inhibition in the absence of lidocaine.
source: Furthermore, while TTX-S currents in neurons from both rat and human were subject to use-dependent inhibition in the absence of lidocaine (Figure 11A,B and D), the inhibition was significantly (p<0.01) greater in rat neurons, at least at 1 and 2 Hz (Figure 11D).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 11.

claim: Use-dependent inhibition of TTX-S currents in the absence of lidocaine was significantly greater in rat neurons than human neurons at 1 and 2 Hz.
source: Furthermore, while TTX-S currents in neurons from both rat and human were subject to use-dependent inhibition in the absence of lidocaine (Figure 11A,B and D), the inhibition was significantly (p<0.01) greater in rat neurons, at least at 1 and 2 Hz (Figure 11D).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 11.

claim: Lidocaine caused significant use-dependent block of TTX-S currents in both human and rat neurons.
source: In both human and rat neurons, lidocaine caused significant (p<0.01) use-dependent block (Figure 11A,B and D).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 11.

claim: No evidence of a low threshold ramp current was detected in human DRG neurons in response to a depolarizing ramp from −100 mV to 0 mV over 500 ms.
source: Despite the presence of TTX-S currents in every neuron included in this analysis, we detected no evidence of a low threshold ramp current in human DRG neurons in response to a depolarizing ramp from −100 mV to 0 mV over 500 ms, following a 500 ms pre-pulse to −90 mV (Figure 12A).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 12A.

claim: Peak inward current evoked in response to the ramp in human DRG neurons was at −5.9 ± 0.6 mV (n = 74).
source: Rather, peak inward current evoked in response to the ramp was at −5.9 ± 0.6 mV (n = 74).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: Little if any detectable suppression of TTX-S currents was observed in response to Pro-Tx II at concentrations as high as 30 nM in 27 human neurons tested.
source: Little if any detectable suppression of TTX-S currents was observed in response to concentrations as high as 30 nM in the 27 neurons tested (Figure 12B).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 12B.

claim: 10 nM Pro-Tx II produced a 50.5 ± 13.7% reduction in TTX-S current in five rat DRG neurons tested.
